2 Algebras, modules and combining systems

Ising fusion over the algebra of sectors Example Chapter 2

Can ordinary vector spaces with their usual tensor product realize the fusion of a specified category? In the semisimple Ising category at central charge 1/21/2, the simple line sectors are the vacuum 11, a fermion ψ\psi, and the spin field σ\sigma. Write ⊠\boxtimes for their fusion. The relevant rules are

ψ⊠ψ=1,ψ⊠σ=σ,σ⊠σ=1⊕︎ψ.\psi\boxtimes\psi=1,\qquad \psi\boxtimes\sigma=\sigma,\qquad \sigma\boxtimes\sigma=1\oplus\psi .

Suppose a faithful additive assignment to finite-dimensional complex vector spaces were to send the vacuum to ℂ\mathbb C and fusion to ordinary tensor product. The first rule would make the fermion space one-dimensional. The last would then require the spin space to have integer dimension dd with d2=2d^2=2.

The obstruction points to what the vector space lost. Test a line XX between an incoming simple sector jj and an outgoing sector ii. The space

VX(i,j)=Hom⁡(i,X⊠j)V_X(i,j)=\operatorname{Hom}(i,X\boxtimes j)

records all such junctions. To compose two junctions one must match the internal sector. If A=ℂ3A=\mathbb C^3 and eie_i is the projector onto sector ii, then the direct sum VX=⨁i,jVX(i,j)V_X=\bigoplus_{i,j}V_X(i,j) is an AA-bimodule. Tensoring it with VYV_Y over AA performs exactly this matching. In the ordinary vector-space tensor product the projection to the matching pairs is

v⊗w⟼∑ivei⊗eiw.v\otimes w\longmapsto\sum_i ve_i\otimes e_iw .

The channel decomposition of Y⊠jY\boxtimes j shows that the relative tensor gives VX⊠YV_{X\boxtimes Y}. The three total dimensions are now 3,3,43,3,4. For instance, with X=σX=\sigma, the incoming sectors 1,ψ,σ1,\psi,\sigma contribute one, one and two junctions respectively. The algebra of the three endomorphism blocks has dimension 32+32+42=343^2+3^2+4^2=34. Its tensor of modules uses the displayed projector and its unit carries all three sector labels. This gives a weak Hopf algebra in the finite reconstruction of Chapter 12. The fusion multiplicities determine the dimensions in this example. Specifying which continuation represents an oriented half-exchange also requires the marked braiding.

4 Factorization and collision geometry

Proposition (ternary diagonal operations) Theorem Chapter 4

For ordinary right differential modules with the fully localized source and unshifted target of (4.3), the linear spans of composites through 12|312|3 and 1|231|23 have zero intersection. Consequently a strictly associative binary operation in these spaces has zero triple products.

Theorem: classical factorization and chiral algebras Theorem Chapter 4, 4.4 Factorization includes the collision extension

The above category of unital factorization algebras is equivalent to the category of unital Beilinson–Drinfeld chiral algebras on XX. The factorization sheaves acquire a canonical differential-module structure, and the corresponding right differential module is ωX⊗B{1}\omega_X\otimes B_{\{1\}}.

Theorem (simultaneous cluster twists) Theorem Chapter 4

Suppose the coincident points at xx form nontrivial blocks S1,…,SbS_1,\ldots,S_b. A positive full twist of a block rotates all its points once around their common centre while leaving the other blocks apart. Let CiC_i be its action on a common fibre EE, using local base paths. Then

Kx≄0⟺⋂i=1bker⁡(Ci−1)dim⁡E≠0.K_x\not\simeq0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \bigcap_{i=1}^b\ker(C_i-1)^{\dim E}\ne0 .

Conjugating the local representation does not change the criterion. The twists commute with each other and with the angular monodromies in this local product, even when the angular monodromies fail to commute among themselves.

A projective line of four-ray attachments Theorem Chapter 4

There is still a choice about attaching the four-point coefficient. Take the transverse slice ℂ3\mathbb C^3, let ii include its origin, and now shift the local system by [3][3] to use the perverse normalization. Put V=H2KV=H^2K and V′=H3KV'=H^3K. For this coefficient P!=j!L[3]P_!=j_!L[3] is perverse. The intermediate extension j!∗L[3]j_{!*}L[3] is the extension with no nonzero subobject or quotient on the boundary. The canonical sequence is

0⟶i∗V⟶P!⟶j!∗L[3]⟶0.0\longrightarrow i_*V\longrightarrow P_! \longrightarrow j_{!*}L[3]\longrightarrow0 .

For each line W⊂VW\subset V, form the quotient PW=P!/(i∗W)P_W=P_!/(i_*W) in the perverse category. Its ordinary stalk is i∗PW≃W[1]i^*P_W\simeq W[1]. The costalk i!PWi^!P_W measures local cohomology supported at the origin. Since i!P!≃K[2]i^!P_!\simeq K[2], the costalk sequence gives H0i!PW=V/WH^0 i^!P_W=V/W and H1i!PW=V′H^1 i^!P_W=V', with all other groups zero.

Every line therefore gives the same ranks and the same extension off the origin. The attaching arrow i∗PW→K[3]i^*P_W\to K[3] on H−1H^{-1} has image the particular line W⊂VW\subset V. Indeed its image is the kernel of the boundary map V→H0i!PW=V/WV\to H^0i^!P_W=V/W. An isomorphism of two such sheaves acts on the separated rank-one local system by a scalar and, by naturality of j!j_!, must carry one embedded kernel in P!P_! to the other. A scalar fixes each line. Hence distinct WW's give distinct isomorphism classes parametrized by ℙ(V)≅ℙ1\mathbb P(V)\cong\mathbb P^1. This calculation concerns extensions on the fixed labelled slice. Identifying a physical collision or an oriented Hall coefficient would require its attaching morphism and compatibility with its other collision maps.

5 Bar constructions and coherent operations

Theorem: connected consecutive-cut duality Theorem Chapter 5, 5.6 Ordered cuts give a finite geometric bar construction

In 𝒲X\mathcal W_X, bar and cobar for consecutive-cut convolution are inverse equivalences between connected augmented coherent associative algebras and connected counital coaugmented coherent coassociative coalgebras. The equivalence includes their full mapping spaces. It requires no cohomological boundedness or finite-dimensionality of coefficients.

Support theorem Theorem Chapter 5, 5.7 The support remembers which cuts were allowed

Consecutive-cut duality restricts to an equivalence between factorizing coalgebras and connected algebras whose positive-arity coefficients vanish on every cut open. For a factorizing coalgebra,

ΩCn≃RΓZn(Cn)[−1].\overline{\Omega C}_n\simeq R\Gamma_{Z_n}(C_n)[-1].

The shift is part of the formula. To see its origin, index a cube by subsets of the n−1n-1 possible cuts. A subset of size r−1r-1 gives rr blocks, hence a cobar term shifted by [−r][-r]. The corresponding localization cube has shift [−(r−1)][-(r-1)]; the two totalizations differ by [−1][-1]. Factorization identifies the entire cut cube with the localization cube, including its maps.

Theorem (the algebraic collision integral) Theorem Chapter 5, 5.8 Rational exchange on all finite collision diagrams

Form GU(V)G_U(V) by taking an algebraic direct sum over chains of surjections, placing a chain of length pp in simplicial degree −p-p, with the usual alternating face maps on the K(I)K(I). Shuffling two chains and concatenating their coefficient words makes GU(V)G_U(V) a unital dg algebra over RR. Its degree-zero cohomology is the intrinsic all-arity mode algebra 𝖬U(V)\mathsf M_U(V).

Recognition theorem Theorem Chapter 7, 7.4 Recognition on Chevalley coalgebras

Suppose VV is any unbounded dg chiral algebra over a characteristic-zero field on 𝔸1\mathbb A^1, with a genuine closed horizontal unit. For every coherent coassociative pointing u:J→CVu:J\to C_V, the maps Θ\Theta and Ψ\Psi are inverse equivalences between 𝒳(CV,u)\mathcal X(C_V,u) and 𝒜C(CV,u)\mathcal A_C(C_V,u). Theorem (four-pole evaluation) Theorem Chapter 8

Over D∗D_* the full four-pole rational resolution has an algebraic evaluation on a resolved model of L∗facL_*^{\mathrm{fac}} for arbitrary constant ordinary pair inputs. Use a separate augmented Y⊗2Y^{\otimes2}-bar for each pair. To see why these bars resolve the stated intersection, contract an acyclic first input over ℂ\mathbb C. Perturb its contraction first by the internal 1212 kernel. A term of order ee contributes qes1−eq^e s_1^{-e} on the radial side and p1ep_1^e in the first completed pair. 9 Ordered boundary operations and mixed theories

Theorem — finite marked Ward calculus Theorem Chapter 9, 9.3 Ordered poles and their complete differential

With the stated compatible flats, internal gates, finite pole and jet orders, upward-proper coefficient support and canonical scalar extension, 𝒟ℳI⊆ℳI\mathcal D\mathcal M_I\subseteq\mathcal M_I. For a scalar coefficient KK with qq marked factors, its derivative consists of four finite sums:

DK=ℬ(K)+𝒮(K)+𝒱(K)+𝒞(K).DK=\mathcal B(K)+\mathcal S(K)+\mathcal V(K)+\mathcal C(K).

Here ℬ\mathcal B replaces a ray by an additional mark with sign (−1)q(-1)^q; 𝒮\mathcal S takes the residues of entire complex-parallel scalar classes; 𝒱\mathcal V takes the oriented real boundaries of whole simplified gates; and 𝒞\mathcal C is the sum over closed critical marked flats. Its coefficients are the annular moments of the whole weighted, gated normal kernel. The derivative of KFKF also includes (−1)qK𝒟F(-1)^qK\mathcal DF. Old normal degrees contribute their Koszul sign, and every residue differentiates the entire remaining coefficient and field family to the required finite normal order.

Theorem (transport of the two-mark contact) Theorem Chapter 9

Adjoin UU, its smooth multiples, finite holomorphic derivatives and full dFd_F-descendants to 𝒱\mathscr V. The continuous cylinder limit on this larger space respects relations of joint currents because it is the ordinary pullback at every positive λ\lambda. A vanishing flux square and its locality obstruction Theorem Chapter 14, 14.1 What a joined interface remembers

What happens if one inserts the flux twice? Write 𝔩=𝔤/ℂ1\mathfrak l=\mathfrak g/\mathbb C1, and lift each polynomial Weyl symbol to its representative with zero constant term. The constant part of the commutator of two lifts is a scalar two-cocycle ω\omega on 𝔩\mathfrak l. Its class acts on the two-sided interval by cap product. Its square vanishes in algebraic cohomology at every numerical ℏ≠0\hbar\ne0, even though its four-input representative is nonzero. For example,

(ω∧ω)(x,y,x3,y3)=3ℏ4.(\omega\wedge\omega)(x,y,x^3,y^3)=3\hbar^4 .

In the Moyal formula the constant coefficient of [xd,yd][x^d,y^d] for odd dd is cd=2d!(ℏ/2)dc_d=2d!(\hbar/2)^d; mixed degrees contribute no constant. The displayed value is 2c1c32c_1c_3.

The primitive comes from cyclic homology of the polynomial Weyl algebra. The normalized Hochschild chain u=ℏ−1x[y]u=\hbar^{-1}x[y] has bu=1bu=1. Its Connes boundary Bu=ℏ−1(1[x|y]−1[y|x])Bu=\hbar^{-1}(1[x|y]-1[y|x]) generates top Hochschild homology and survives in cyclic degree two. Thus the unit gives a nonzero ordinary cyclic degree-two class. Choose an algebraic cyclic two-cocycle Φ\Phi on unnormalized chains with Φ(1,1,1)=1\Phi(1,1,1)=1. Antisymmetrizing Φ\Phi gives a closed Lie three-cochain on 𝔤\mathfrak g. For the chosen lift s:𝔩→𝔤s:\mathfrak l\to\mathfrak g, let PP be its restriction to the three lifted inputs and put β(a)=Φ(1,1,sa)\beta(a)=\Phi(1,1,sa). The cyclic cocycle identity gives dP=ω∧(ω−dβ)dP=\omega\wedge(\omega-d\beta). Hence H=P+ω∧βH=P+\omega\wedge\beta satisfies dH=ω∧ωdH=\omega\wedge\omega. Contraction by HH gives a bimodule homotopy for the two successive cap operations. At rank one, where the cap in degree two is an isomorphism, the component of the outgoing cut from degree four to two degree-two factors is zero. The higher Tor groups themselves are not determined by this identity.

This calculation places a real condition on a proposed physical junction. For every fixed spatial jet order LL, choose different odd d,e>Ld,e>L. A trilinear primitive factoring through the order-LL Taylor jet of each input would have zero differential on xd,yd,xe,yex^d,y^d,x^e,y^e. Even after taking one bracket, two untouched inputs still have zero jets. Yet the marked square has value 2cdce≠02c_dc_e\ne0. The algebraic primitive can use arbitrarily high jets on polynomial inputs. An independent field theory would have to construct its two endpoint actions, preserve the cap and outgoing cut, and supply a contact homotopy in its own allowed space of distributions. Which jet orders and regularization it admits is a physical input.

Glossary

Each definition as its chapter gives it, with a link to its place in the chapter.

Actor and pointing Defined in Chapter 7, 7.3 A factorizing actor and its pointing

We call such a coalgebra an actor when it parametrizes operations on another object. The word does not add a multiplication to FF. Two tensor products occur. Disjoint convolution, written ⋆\star, combines configurations by splitting their labels; its unit KK is concentrated at the empty configuration. The tensor ⊗!\otimes^! combines two coefficient systems at the same configuration by extraordinary pullback along the diagonal. Its unit JJ has the local unit coefficient at each configuration. A pointing is an actual coherent coalgebra map

u:J⟶F.u:J\longrightarrow F.

It specifies a vacuum operation together with all its compatibility homotopies. It contains more information than a class in the singleton cohomology. These conventions are those of the ordered-collision coalgebra construction, particularly its coalgebra category and diagonal tensor.

The smallest useful test algebra has two orthogonal idempotents:

B=kp1⊕︎kp2,pipj=δijpi.B=kp_1\oplus kp_2,\qquad p_ip_j=\delta_{ij}p_i.

Let C=CBC=C_B be its Chevalley coalgebra: its coefficients are built from finite partitions with a BB-label on each block, and its differential merges blocks using the product of BB. It has multiplication m:C⊗!C→Cm:C\otimes^!C\to C and total unit pointing uB:J→Cu_B:J\to C. The two idempotents distinguish two colours of input and output.

A character of (F,u)(F,u) is a coalgebra map g:F→Cg:F\to C together with a specified homotopy gu≃uBgu\simeq u_B. An action is a coalgebra map α:F⊗!C→C\alpha:F\otimes^!C\to C together with a specified homotopy α(u⊗!1C)≃1C\alpha(u\otimes^!1_C)\simeq1_C. There is no additional associative-action axiom involving a multiplication on FF. To retain the specified homotopies and homotopies between them, define the complete spaces

𝒳(F,u)=hofibuB⁡[MapCoalg⁡(F,C)→u∗MapCoalg⁡(J,C)],𝒜C(F,u)=hofib1C⁡[MapCoalg⁡(F⊗!C,C)→(u⊗!1C)∗MapCoalg⁡(C,C)].\begin{aligned} \mathcal X(F,u) &=\operatorname{hofib}_{u_B}\left[ \operatorname{Map}_{\mathrm{Coalg}}(F,C) \xrightarrow{u^*}\operatorname{Map}_{\mathrm{Coalg}}(J,C)\right],\\ \mathcal A_C(F,u) &=\operatorname{hofib}_{1_C}\left[ \operatorname{Map}_{\mathrm{Coalg}}(F\otimes^!C,C) \xrightarrow{(u\otimes^!1_C)^*}\operatorname{Map}_{\mathrm{Coalg}}(C,C)\right]. \end{aligned}

A homotopy fibre records a point upstairs and a path from its image to the specified base point; its higher simplices record the remaining compatibilities.

Adjunction Defined in Chapter 6, 6.1 What the unit and counit measure

Let AA be another dg algebra and let WW be an AA-BB bimodule. Derived tensor and derived Hom give an adjunction

Φ=W⊗B𝐋−:D(B)⇄D(A):Ψ=RHomA⁡(W,−).\Phi=W\otimes_B^{\mathbf L}-:D(B) \rightleftarrows D(A): \Psi=\operatorname{RHom}_A(W,-).

Its defining property is the natural equivalence

RHomA⁡(ΦL,M)≃RHomB⁡(L,ΨM).\operatorname{RHom}_A(\Phi L,M) \simeq\operatorname{RHom}_B(L,\Psi M).

The unit ηL:L→ΨΦL\eta_L:L\to\Psi\Phi L corresponds to the identity of ΦL\Phi L; the counit εM:ΦΨM→M\varepsilon_M:\Phi\Psi M\to M corresponds to the identity of ΨM\Psi M. In degree zero the counit is evaluation. Derived resolutions supply its meaning on complexes. These are adjunction maps, distinct from an algebra unit or a coalgebra counit.

The two triangle identities are

εΦL∘Φ(ηL)=1ΦL,Ψ(εM)∘ηΨM=1ΨM.\varepsilon_{\Phi L}\circ\Phi(\eta_L)=1_{\Phi L}, \qquad \Psi(\varepsilon_M)\circ\eta_{\Psi M}=1_{\Psi M}.

They express compatibility of the two reconstructions. The functor Φ\Phi is fully faithful precisely when every ηL\eta_L is an equivalence. The functor Ψ\Psi is fully faithful precisely when every εM\varepsilon_M is an equivalence. An equivalence of the two whole categories requires both.

In degree zero the counit is evaluation. Derived resolutions supply its meaning on complexes. These are adjunction maps, distinct from an algebra unit or a coalgebra counit.

Algebra Defined in Chapter 2, 2.1 Multiplication and representations

A unital associative algebra consists of a vector space AA, a bilinear multiplication m:A⊗A→Am:A\otimes A\to A, and an element 1A1_A such that

(ab)c=a(bc),1Aa=a=a1A.(ab)c=a(bc),\qquad 1_Aa=a=a1_A.

Equivalently, the unit is a linear map uA:k→Au_A:k\to A, uA(1)=1Au_A(1)=1_A. For an algebra of operators, associativity is the statement that three successive operations have a well-defined composite.

A left AA-module is a vector space MM together with an action ρM:A⊗M→M\rho_M:A\otimes M\to M satisfying

(ab)m=a(bm),1Am=m.(ab)m=a(bm),\qquad 1_Am=m.

A map of modules f:M→Nf:M\to N is a linear map with f(am)=af(m)f(am)=af(m). Such a map compares the systems together with their observable actions, not merely their underlying vector spaces.

For example, let A=k[x]A=k[x]. For every λ∈k\lambda\in k, there is a one-dimensional module kλk_\lambda on which xx acts by multiplication by λ\lambda. A module map f:kλ→kμf:k_\lambda\to k_\mu must satisfy

λf(1)=μf(1).\lambda f(1)=\mu f(1).

Thus kλk_\lambda and kμk_\mu are isomorphic precisely when λ=μ\lambda=\mu. Their dimensions agree for every pair of parameters. A counting invariant of the state space has discarded the action that distinguishes them.

Associative chiral algebra Defined in Chapter 12, 12.1 Associative products on configurations

For either specified convolution, an associative chiral algebra is an augmented E1E_1-algebra AA with positive augmentation ideal whose bar coalgebra BABA factorizes. This means that each specified coproduct component restricts to an equivalence with the external product of the block coefficients on its separating open. In the word category the decompositions are consecutive cuts; on the ordered collision atlas they are arbitrary ordered decompositions into subsets. The coefficient category, convolution and componentwise factorization condition are part of the definition. [CQ1]

Associator Defined in Chapter 2, 2.5 Associators, exchange and coherence

Even when tensor products are associative up to canonical isomorphism, the isomorphisms must agree with one another. For three objects there is an associator

αL,M,N:(L⊗M)⊗N⟶L⊗(M⊗N).\alpha_{L,M,N}:(L\otimes M)\otimes N \longrightarrow L\otimes(M\otimes N).

For four objects, the pentagon identity says that the two paths from

((L⊗M)⊗N)⊗PtoL⊗(M⊗(N⊗P))((L\otimes M)\otimes N)\otimes P \quad\text{to}\quad L\otimes(M\otimes(N\otimes P))

agree. One path uses two associators; the other uses three. This is an equation of maps, not merely an assertion that the initial and final objects are isomorphic.

A braiding is a natural family of isomorphisms

βM,N:M⊗N⟶N⊗M,\beta_{M,N}:M\otimes N\longrightarrow N\otimes M,

compatible with maps of both input objects. It has its own compatibility with composition. With parentheses identified by the associator, its two hexagon equations read

βL,M⊗N=(idM⊗βL,N)(βL,M⊗idN),\beta_{L,M\otimes N} =(\mathrm{id}_M\otimes\beta_{L,N}) (\beta_{L,M}\otimes\mathrm{id}_N),
(2.9)
βL⊗M,N=(βL,N⊗idM)(idL⊗βM,N).\beta_{L\otimes M,N} =(\beta_{L,N}\otimes\mathrm{id}_M) (\mathrm{id}_L\otimes\beta_{M,N}).
(2.10)

These equations say that moving one object past a pair agrees with moving it past the two factors successively.

Attaching map Defined in Chapter 17, 17.6 Independent realizations test what reconstruction preserves

An attaching map makes the remaining choices concrete. If j:U↪Xj:U\hookrightarrow X is the complement of a closed point ii, fix a coefficient LL on UU and a complex VV on the point. A map V→i∗Rj∗LV\to i^*Rj_*L specifies how the value on the point sees the punctured neighbourhood. The corresponding constructible sheaf is the homotopy pullback

Rj∗L×i∗i∗Rj∗Lhi∗V.Rj_*L\mathop{\times}^{h}_{i_*i^*Rj_*L} i_*V .

Restriction to UU recovers LL, and restriction to the point recovers VV. Restricting the projection from the glued sheaf to Rj∗LRj_*L gives the chosen arrow from VV to the link. For the four charge-one rays at level two, different lines in the two-dimensional degree-two cohomology of the deepest link, H2(i∗Rj∗L)H^2(i^*Rj_*L), give genuinely different perverse extensions with identical stalk and costalk dimensions. For identical rays, fix the coordinate framings and specify the positive half-exchange as +i+i. With that linearization the permutation action on H2(i∗Rj∗L)H^2(i^*Rj_*L) splits as the trivial character plus the sign character. Exactly their two lines in the projective family admit this equivariance. If the coefficient is further required to be the ordinary inverse image of a sheaf on the coarse unordered space, every stabilizer must act trivially on each stalk. This singles out the quotient by the trivial line, the pullback of the downstairs middle extension. The physical theory would have to supply that last requirement or decide between the two equivariant candidates in another way. The four-point attachment

Bar construction Defined in Chapter 5, 5.3 Words and the reduced bar construction

An augmentation of a unital dg algebra is a dg algebra map ϵ:A→k\epsilon:A\to k, where kk is the ground field. It splits the underlying complex as A=k⋅1⊕︎A‾A=k\cdot1\oplus\bar A, with A‾=ker⁡ϵ\bar A=\ker\epsilon. The reduced bar construction, including its empty word, is

BA=Tc(A‾[1])=k⊕︎⨁n≥1(A‾[1])⊗n.BA=T^c(\bar A[1]) =k\oplus\bigoplus_{n\ge1}(\bar A[1])^{\otimes n}.

We write

[a1|⋯|an]=sa1⊗⋯⊗san,|[a1|⋯|an]|=∑i|ai|−n.[a_1|\cdots|a_n]=sa_1\otimes\cdots\otimes sa_n, \qquad |[a_1|\cdots|a_n]|=\sum_i|a_i|-n.

The superscript cc indicates the tensor coalgebra. Its coproduct splits a word at every position:

Δ[a1|⋯|an]=∑i=0n[a1|⋯|ai]⊗[ai+1|⋯|an].\Delta[a_1|\cdots|a_n] =\sum_{i=0}^n[a_1|\cdots|a_i] \otimes[a_{i+1}|\cdots|a_n].

The empty word is 11. This deconcatenation is coassociative because splitting at two positions gives the same three consecutive subwords in either order.

The bar differential has two kinds of terms. It applies the differential of AA to one letter, or multiplies two adjacent letters. With our cohomological suspension convention, its defining components are

b1(sa)=−s(da),b2(sa⊗sb)=(−1)|a|s(ab).b_1(sa)=-s(da),\qquad b_2(sa\otimes sb)=(-1)^{|a|}s(ab).

They extend to words by applying the operation in each possible position. Passing a degree-one operation across a prefix contributes the degree of that prefix. Explicitly,

b[a1|⋯|an]=∑i=1n(−1)1+∑j<i(|aj|−1)[a1|⋯|dai|⋯|an]+∑i=1n−1(−1)|ai|+∑j<i(|aj|−1)[a1|⋯|aiai+1|⋯|an].\begin{aligned} b[a_1|\cdots|a_n] ={}&\sum_{i=1}^n (-1)^{1+\sum_{j<i}(|a_j|-1)} [a_1|\cdots|da_i|\cdots|a_n]\\ &+\sum_{i=1}^{n-1} (-1)^{|a_i|+\sum_{j<i}(|a_j|-1)} [a_1|\cdots|a_ia_{i+1}|\cdots|a_n]. \end{aligned}

The equation b2=0b^2=0 expresses three familiar facts: d2=0d^2=0, the Leibniz rule, and associativity. For an ordinary algebra concentrated in degree zero, the internal-differential terms vanish, and

b[a|b]=[ab],b[a|b|c]=[ab|c]−[a|bc].b[a|b]=[ab],\qquad b[a|b|c]=[ab|c]-[a|bc].

Applying bb again gives [(ab)c]−[a(bc)]=0[(ab)c]-[a(bc)]=0. The length-three word makes the relation between the two multiplications into an explicit boundary equation. Longer words organize the compatible ways of repeating this operation. These are the usual algebraic bar formulas, expressed in cohomological degrees; see Loday–Vallette, Algebraic Operads, §§2.2–2.3.

Bialgebra Defined in Chapter 2, 2.2 A coproduct gives the action on a tensor product

(ϵ⊗id)Δ=id=(id⊗ϵ)Δ.(\epsilon\otimes\mathrm{id})\Delta =\mathrm{id} =(\mathrm{id}\otimes\epsilon)\Delta.
(2.4)

The map ϵ\epsilon is the coalgebra counit. An algebra HH with Δ\Delta and ϵ\epsilon satisfying (2.2)–(2.4) is a bialgebra.

Braiding Defined in Chapter 2, 2.5 Associators, exchange and coherence

A braiding is a natural family of isomorphisms

βM,N:M⊗N⟶N⊗M,\beta_{M,N}:M\otimes N\longrightarrow N\otimes M,

compatible with maps of both input objects. It has its own compatibility with composition. With parentheses identified by the associator, its two hexagon equations read

βL,M⊗N=(idM⊗βL,N)(βL,M⊗idN),\beta_{L,M\otimes N} =(\mathrm{id}_M\otimes\beta_{L,N}) (\beta_{L,M}\otimes\mathrm{id}_N),
(2.9)
βL⊗M,N=(βL,N⊗idM)(idL⊗βM,N).\beta_{L\otimes M,N} =(\beta_{L,N}\otimes\mathrm{id}_M) (\mathrm{id}_L\otimes\beta_{M,N}).
(2.10)

These equations say that moving one object past a pair agrees with moving it past the two factors successively.

For ordinary vector spaces, the flip provides such a braiding. For HH-modules it is action-preserving when the coproduct is cocommutative, meaning τΔ=Δ\tau\Delta=\Delta. A noncocommutative coproduct requires additional data to obtain an exchange map. In local field theories, the exchange can also depend on positions and continuation paths. The associator and hexagon equations then become part of the comparison to be proved.

Here coherence means these specified compatibility equations. For complexes, some equalities are replaced by homotopies, which must satisfy further equations of their own. Retaining an associator without its pentagon, or a binary homotopy without the next compatibility, retains only part of the structure.

Brane and BRST differential Defined in Chapter 14

The word open refers to fields attached to a brane, and closed to bulk fields that can couple to them. After choosing a square-zero supersymmetry, both sectors are described by complexes. Gauge symmetry is incorporated by a Becchi–Rouet–Stora–Tyutin, or BRST, differential, with additional ghost variables recording gauge transformations and their relations. The research question is whether an independently defined bulk action can be compared with the boundary's derived operations, including junction composition and higher products. Several exact comparisons below answer parts of this question. Their coefficient rings and fields differ, so the comparison between the physical theories must itself be constructed.

Cap Defined in Chapter 17, 17.5 States and amplitudes impose another comparison

A cap is a chosen filling of a boundary together with fields, boundary conditions and normalization that prepare a vector or functional in the specified boundary state space. If an anomaly makes the amplitude line-valued, that line belongs to the data. For a bulk observable OO, an exact cap comparison would take the form

ZMbulk(O)=ZM∂(rM(O)),Z_M^{\mathrm{bulk}}(O) =Z_M^{\partial}\bigl(r_M(O)\bigr),
(17.9)

where rMr_M is the actual observable comparison and both sides take values in an identified amplitude line. This equation is a target, not a definition of ZM∂Z_M^{\partial} by the left-hand side. The state prepared by the filling must be constructed independently, and the comparison must commute with cutting and gluing.

Cauchy lift of a matrix current Defined in Chapter 12

Let eij=ℓij[0]e_{ij}=\ell_{ij}^{[0]} be the matrix-current states. The Cauchy lift of a current mode begins with the one-position mode of eije_{ij}. At first order its creation correction for Laurent multiplier ff is

−ℏ∑a[f(x)/(x−y);eia,eaj].-\hbar\sum_a [f(x)/(x-y);e_{ia},e_{aj}] .

Centre Defined in Chapter 7, 7.1 Central operations on modules

Let AA be a unital associative algebra over a characteristic-zero field kk. Its centre is

Z(A)={z∈A:za=az for every a∈A}.Z(A)=\{z\in A:za=az\text{ for every }a\in A\}.

For every left AA-module MM, a central element gives an AA-linear operator m↦zmm\mapsto zm, naturally in MM. Conversely, every natural endomorphism of the identity functor on AA-modules arises this way. Indeed, its value on the regular module is determined by z=ηA(1)z=\eta_A(1). Naturality with respect to right multiplication by aa gives az=zaaz=za; naturality with respect to A→M,b↦bmA\to M, b\mapsto bm, then gives ηM(m)=zm\eta_M(m)=zm.

Thus the same element acts compatibly on every representation. This explains why a centre is relevant to bulk–boundary questions: an operation that can be moved without changing its interaction with boundary observables should produce compatible operators on boundary representations. Additional geometric structure is needed to turn this motivation into a statement about a field theory.

Charge measured by a current contour Defined in Chapter 3

The vacuum contraction used above cannot determine the charge of a line ending on the boundary. To see the charge, integrate the current around the endpoint. In our indexing the coefficient picked out by (2πi)−1∮J(z)dz(2\pi i)^{-1}\oint J(z)\,dz is J0J_0. In abelian Chern–Simons theory on the half-space take a proper oriented Wilson ray of charge aa, fix the boundary complex coordinate and let k≠0k\ne0 be the numerical boundary current level. The source couples the ray to the integral of the gauge one-form. For the local Fock calculation take the ray straight in the endpoint half-ball, with a moving graph ray vertical near the current tests. On that half-ball the change of source shifts the contour mode by aa. On the part of the cohomology spanned by finite angular weights the result is

ℱa=ℂ[x1,x2,…]|a⟩,J−n=xn,Jn=kn∂xn (n>0),J0=a.\mathcal F_a=\mathbb C[x_1,x_2,\ldots]|a\rangle,\qquad J_{-n}=x_n,\quad J_n=kn\partial_{x_n}\ (n>0),\quad J_0=a .

Thus the very same double-pole relation holds for every charge. The contour distinguishes two charges which any measurement using only that pole would identify.

Chiral coproduct Defined in Chapter 12, 12.1 Associative products on configurations

A compatible E1E_1 chiral coproduct requires further data. Specify a tensor product ⋄\diamond combining systems at the same positions, together with the geometric interchange that makes A⋄A′A\diamond A' an algebra for ⋆\star. A coproduct is then an algebra map

D:A⟶A⋄AD:A\longrightarrow A\diamond A

with coassociativity and a counit to the ⋄\diamond-unit, or a level-indexed family of such maps. In a derived formulation these include the indicated homotopies and their higher identities. They are not supplied by naming two binary arrows.

The familiar bialgebra identity illustrates the required interchange:

Δμ=(μ⊗μ)(1⊗τ⊗1)(Δ⊗Δ).\Delta\mu=(\mu\otimes\mu) (1\otimes\tau\otimes1)(\Delta\otimes\Delta).

Here τ\tau exchanges the middle two factors, and the unit and counit must also be compatible. In chiral geometry the corresponding square uses the actual configuration extensions and same-position tensor. Its arrows must be defined on their pole and support domains. For instance, diagonal tensor of collision coalgebras transports through bar–cobar to

A⋄A′=Ω(BA⊗!BA′).A\diamond A'=\Omega(BA\otimes^!BA').

This construction does not automatically identify ⋄\diamond with a tensor of fields carrying a nontrivial exchange. The latter needs its own comparison. [CQ1, CQ2]

The construction from a Beilinson–Drinfeld chiral Lie algebra LL is

L⟼Cch(L)⟼rescut⁡Cch(L)⟼Ωcutrescut⁡Cch(L).L\longmapsto C_{\mathrm{ch}}(L) \longmapsto\operatorname{res}_{\mathrm{cut}}C_{\mathrm{ch}}(L) \longmapsto\Omega_{\mathrm{cut}}\operatorname{res}_{\mathrm{cut}}C_{\mathrm{ch}}(L).

Here CchC_{\mathrm{ch}} is the Francis–Gaitsgory chiral Chevalley-chain construction. Its coalgebra is cocommutative for the chiral tensor on Ran space and factorizes when the Lie object is supported on the singleton copy of XX. The operation rescut⁡\operatorname{res}_{\mathrm{cut}} retains only monotone collision maps and projects the all-subset coproduct onto consecutive cuts. Coassociativity survives because both iterated projections retain the same consecutive blocks; factorization survives on the cut opens. Taking associative cobar then gives the word object defined above.

This comparison is performed on the coalgebra before taking cobar. It does not identify associative bar–cobar duality with Lie–commutative duality. To recover a chiral Lie algebra in the reverse direction, the entire associative bar must extend along every finite-set surjection with a compatible cocommutative coproduct and factorization. A field comparison and a chiral coproduct require their additional vacuum and tensor data. [CQ1, CQ3]

Chiral operation Defined in Chapter 4, 4.2 A chiral operation is a map with a collision target

The direct image ΔI∗M\Delta_{I*}M is a differential module on XIX^I supported on the small diagonal. It includes derivatives in directions normal to that diagonal. A chiral II-operation is a differential-module map

μ:jI∗jI∗(⊠i∈ILi)⟶ΔI∗M.\mu: j_{I*}j_I^*\Bigl(\boxtimes_{i\in I}L_i\Bigr) \longrightarrow\Delta_{I*}M.
(4.3)

Thus its space is

PIch((Li);M)=Hom𝒟XI⁡(jI∗jI∗⊠iLi,ΔI∗M).P_I^{\mathrm{ch}}((L_i);M) =\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal D_{X^I}} \left(j_{I*}j_I^*\boxtimes_iL_i,\Delta_{I*}M\right).
(4.4)

Both sides of the Hom belong to the same category on XIX^I. The source permits separated inputs and their poles; the target records an output concentrated at their collision. This is the operation space of Beilinson–Drinfeld, Chiral Algebras, §3.1.1.

The simplest model is a residue. With a local normal coordinate t=z−wt=z-w, the functional associated to a pole of order rr acts on a test series f(t)f(t) by

Rest=0⁡f(t)trdt=f(r−1)(0)(r−1)!.\operatorname{Res}_{t=0}\frac{f(t)}{t^r}\,dt =\frac{f^{(r-1)}(0)}{(r-1)!}.
(4.5)

A simple pole extracts a value; a double pole extracts a first derivative. Higher poles retain higher normal derivatives. The target in (4.3) is designed to hold this information. Substituting z=wz=w into a singular function would not define the operation.

For three inputs, one can compose a binary operation on the first block with a second binary operation on its output and the remaining input. The partition open UπU_\pi keeps distinct clusters apart during the first step. Localization and the diagonal direct-image identities then place the composite in PJchP_J^{\mathrm{ch}}. These composition maps are associative. Beilinson–Drinfeld, §3.1.2, writes them for arbitrary surjections of finite sets; the geometry explains the intermediate domains that a bare expression such as μ(μ(a,b),c)\mu(\mu(a,b),c) suppresses.

Cobar construction Defined in Chapter 5, 5.5 Cobar reverses the construction

The cobar construction is the tensor algebra

ΩC=T(C‾[−1]).\Omega C=T(\bar C[-1]).

Write ucuc for a generator in C‾[−1]\bar C[-1], so |uc|=|c|+1|uc|=|c|+1. If Δ‾c=∑c′⊗c′′\bar\Delta c=\sum c'\otimes c'', its differential is the derivation determined by

dΩ(uc)=−u(dCc)+∑(−1)|c′|+1(uc′)(uc′′).d_\Omega(uc)=-u(d_Cc) +\sum(-1)^{|c'|+1}(uc')(uc'').

Thus bar shortens words by multiplication, while cobar lengthens them by coproduct. The signs are compatible: when a,ba,b have degree zero, the generator u[a|b]u[a|b] in ΩBA\Omega BA satisfies

dΩu[a|b]=−u[ab]+(u[a])(u[b]).d_\Omega u[a|b]=-u[ab]+(u[a])(u[b]).

The map ΩBA→A\Omega BA\to A sending u[a]u[a] to aa and the longer single generators to zero respects this equation. Its extra generators explicitly encode the multiplication relations in AA.

More generally, a degree-one map τ:C→A\tau:C\to A, vanishing on the coaugmentation and landing in A‾\bar A, is a twisting cochain when

dAτ+τdC+μA(τ⊗τ)Δ‾=0.d_A\tau+\tau d_C+\mu_A(\tau\otimes\tau)\bar\Delta=0.

Here (τ⊗τ)(c′⊗c′′)=(−1)|c′|τ(c′)⊗τ(c′′)(\tau\otimes\tau)(c'\otimes c'')=(-1)^{|c'|}\tau(c')\otimes\tau(c''). This one equation says exactly that uc↦τ(c)uc\mapsto\tau(c) extends to a dg algebra map ΩC→A\Omega C\to A. For conilpotent CC, iterating its reduced coproduct gives the corresponding dg coalgebra map C→BAC\to BA. We obtain the strict bar–cobar adjunction

HomdgAlg⁡(ΩC,A)≅Tw⁡(C,A)≅HomdgCoalg⁡(C,BA).\operatorname{Hom}_{\rm dgAlg}(\Omega C,A) \cong\operatorname{Tw}(C,A) \cong\operatorname{Hom}_{\rm dgCoalg}(C,BA).

An adjunction provides comparison maps. Whether those maps are equivalences requires a theorem about the objects and weak equivalences under consideration. The geometry of ordered configurations supplies an especially useful finiteness condition for such a theorem.

Cochain complex Defined in Chapter 5, 5.1 Complexes retain the equations and their solutions

A cochain complex is a sequence of vector spaces and linear maps

⋯⟶Vn−1→dVn→dVn+1⟶⋯,d2=0.\cdots\longrightarrow V^{n-1}\xrightarrow{d}V^n \xrightarrow{d}V^{n+1}\longrightarrow\cdots, \qquad d^2=0.

The superscript is the cohomological degree, and the differential has degree +1+1. A vector killed by dd is a cycle; a vector of the form dwdw is a boundary. Their quotient is

Hn(V)=ker⁡(d:Vn→Vn+1)/im⁡(d:Vn−1→Vn).H^n(V)=\ker(d:V^n\to V^{n+1})/ \operatorname{im}(d:V^{n-1}\to V^n).

The distinction between a boundary and a chosen primitive matters. Knowing that v=dwv=dw is solvable does not specify ww, and different choices can enter later operations.

Our shift convention is

V[1]n=Vn+1,dV[1]=−dV.V[1]^n=V^{n+1},\qquad d_{V[1]}=-d_V.

Thus a vector of degree rr in VV has degree r−1r-1 in V[1]V[1]. Write svsv for that shifted vector; ss has degree −1-1. Tensor products use the Koszul sign rule:

d(v⊗w)=dv⊗w+(−1)|v|v⊗dw,d(v\otimes w)=dv\otimes w+(-1)^{|v|}v\otimes dw,

where |v||v| denotes the degree of a homogeneous vector.

A chain map f:V→Wf:V\to W commutes with the differentials. A homotopy from gg to ff is a degree-minus-one map hh satisfying

f−g=dWh+hdV.f-g=d_Wh+hd_V.

Homotopic maps induce the same cohomology map, but the homotopy contains information that this induced map forgets. More generally, maps of all degrees form a complex

Homr⁡(V,W)=∏nHom⁡(Vn,Wn+r),∂f=dWf−(−1)rfdV.\operatorname{Hom}^r(V,W)=\prod_n\operatorname{Hom}(V^n,W^{n+r}), \qquad \partial f=d_Wf-(-1)^rfd_V.

Chain maps are its degree-zero cycles, and homotopies identify maps whose difference is a boundary. The product over nn is intentional: a degree-rr map has a component on every degree of VV.

A chain map is a quasi-isomorphism if it induces an isomorphism on every cohomology group. The ordinary derived category formally makes these maps invertible. We will also retain the derived mapping complexes, obtained by resolving the inputs as necessary, rather than keeping only their degree-zero cohomology. This enhanced form of the derived category remembers homotopies and homotopies between them; it is the meaning intended when the geometric theorem below refers to higher mapping spaces.

Coherent associative algebra Defined in Chapter 5, 5.4 One differential encodes all associativity homotopies

The word complex also accommodates multiplication that is associative only through specified homotopies. A degree-one map bb on Tc(V[1])T^c(V[1]) is a coderivation if

Δb=(b⊗1+1⊗b)Δ,\Delta b=(b\otimes1+1\otimes b)\Delta,

with the graded tensor convention. Such a map is determined by its components

bn:(V[1])⊗n⟶V[1].b_n:(V[1])^{\otimes n}\longrightarrow V[1].

On a finite word only finitely many components can act. An uncurved A∞A_\infty-algebra structure is a coderivation with no constant component and with b2=0b^2=0. Undoing the shifts gives operations mn:V⊗n→Vm_n:V^{\otimes n}\to V of degree 2−n2-n. The suspended formulation fixes the signs without a separate convention for every arity.

Compact object Defined in Chapter 6, 6.6 The image and its original counit

An object is compact in a category if maps from it commute with arbitrary coproducts. The free module BB is compact in D(B)D(B), so WW is compact inside 𝒞\mathscr C, with all shifts included when graded. Compactness against arbitrary smooth targets would require an additional statement about Ψ\Psi on coproducts in the ambient category.

Conditional expectation Defined in Chapter 1, 1.1 Reduction must retain the measurements

For a polynomial f(x,y)f(x,y), write this rule as conditional expectation:

ℰ(f)(x)=Zy(x)−1∫ℝf(x,y)e−S(x,y)/ℏdy.\mathcal E(f)(x) =Z_y(x)^{-1} \int_{\mathbb R} f(x,y)e^{-S(x,y)/\hbar}\,dy.

It is linear and preserves the constant observable, but it is generally not multiplicative. Equations (1.2) give

ℰ(y2)−ℰ(y)2=ℏb.\mathcal E(y^2)-\mathcal E(y)^2=\frac{\hbar}{b}.
(1.3)

An effective theory therefore needs to explain how products are transported. In field theory the analogous correction is a contraction of fields. With many insertions, the corrections must also agree when the same reduction is performed in different orders.

Configuration space Defined in Chapter 4, 4.1 Configurations and partial diagonals

Let XX be a smooth algebraic curve over a characteristic-zero field kk. For a finite nonempty set II, the product XIX^I records an II-labelled family of points. Its open configuration space is

UI={(xi)∈XI:xi≠xj whenever i≠j}.U_I=\{(x_i)\in X^I:x_i\ne x_j\text{ whenever }i\ne j\}.
(4.1)

Write jI:UI↪XIj_I:U_I\hookrightarrow X^I for its inclusion. The small diagonal is the map

ΔI:X⟶XI,x⟼(x)i∈I.\Delta_I:X\longrightarrow X^I, \qquad x\longmapsto(x)_{i\in I}.

Its image is the locus where all the labelled points coincide. For two labels i,ji,j, the partial diagonal Δij\Delta_{ij} imposes only xi=xjx_i=x_j.

A partition of the labels specifies which points are to be treated as one cluster. Represent it by a surjection π:J↠I\pi:J\twoheadrightarrow I, with blocks Ji=π−1(i)J_i=\pi^{-1}(i). Define

Uπ={(xj)∈XJ:xj≠xj′ if π(j)≠π(j′)}.U_\pi=\{(x_j)\in X^J: x_j\ne x_{j'}\text{ if }\pi(j)\ne\pi(j')\}.
(4.2)

Points in different blocks must be distinct; points in the same block may collide. The associated diagonal map

Δπ:XI⟶XJ,(xi)⟼(xπ(j))\Delta_\pi:X^I\longrightarrow X^J, \qquad(x_i)\longmapsto(x_{\pi(j)})

inserts one repeated coordinate for every label in a block. Its image is the locus where the points in each block coincide.

Conilpotent coalgebra Defined in Chapter 5, 5.5 Cobar reverses the construction

Let C=k⊕︎C‾C=k\oplus\bar C be a coaugmented dg coalgebra. Its reduced coproduct is Δ‾:C‾→C‾⊗C‾\bar\Delta:\bar C\to\bar C\otimes\bar C, obtained by removing the two terms involving 11. The coalgebra is conilpotent if sufficiently many iterated reduced coproducts kill each element. The tensor coalgebra above has this property because a word cannot be split into more nonempty pieces than its length.

Consecutive cut Defined in Chapter 4, 4.6 Ordered points lead to a different support

For the word construction, retain the external label order 1,…,n1,\ldots,n. This orders the inputs; it imposes no real order on points of the complex curve. A monotone surjection collapses consecutive labels, and the coefficient complexes carry coherent extraordinary-pullback identifications along its diagonal map. Only adjacent repetitions disappear from a word: (x,y,x)(x,y,x) with x≠yx\ne y retains the middle insertion. A consecutive cut after the pp-th input separates the blocks {1,…,p}\{1,\ldots,p\} and {p+1,…,n}\{p+1,\ldots,n\}. Its open set is

Up,n−p={(xi):xi≠xj whenever i≤p<j}.U_{p,n-p}= \{(x_i):x_i\ne x_j\text{ whenever }i\leq p<j\}.
(4.9)

Collisions within either block are allowed. These are the opens used by the consecutive-cut tensor product in Chapter 5.

Contramodule Defined in Chapter 12, 12.4 Nonlinear fields: the W3W_3 example

A graded contramodule is a graded vector space QQ with a degree-zero contraaction γ:𝕋Bc(Q)→Q\gamma:\mathbb T_{B_c}(Q)\to Q satisfying

γηQ=1Q,γ𝕋Bc(γ)=γmQ.\gamma\eta_Q=1_Q,\qquad \gamma\mathbb T_{B_c}(\gamma)=\gamma m_Q.

Thus γ\gamma evaluates the permitted infinite sums. A curved differential graded contramodule additionally has a degree-one connection DQD_Q satisfying the Leibniz rule for all these sums and

DQ(bq)=d(b)q+(−1)|b|bDQ(q),DQ2(q)=hq.D_Q(bq)=d(b)q+(-1)^{|b|}bD_Q(q),\qquad D_Q^2(q)=hq.

These objects and their graded contramodule maps form the differential graded category CDGContra⁡(Bc)\operatorname{CDGContra}(B_c), with differential f↦DQ′f−(−1)|f|fDQf\mapsto D_{Q'}f-(-1)^{|f|}fD_Q on maps Q→Q′Q\to Q'. An arbitrary QQ is not assigned a topology: its summations are the contraaction, whereas the specified free objects have the displayed inverse-limit topology.

Writing Ch⁡(𝒮c)\operatorname{Ch}(\mathcal S_c) for complexes in the category of smooth modules, there are actual differential graded adjoint functors

Kc:Ch⁡(𝒮c)⇄CDGContra⁡(Bc):Fc,K_c:\operatorname{Ch}(\mathcal S_c) \rightleftarrows \operatorname{CDGContra}(B_c):F_c,

The free-on-degree-zero objects with smooth recovered action characterize 𝒮c\mathcal S_c exactly. For every pair of smooth modules, the iterated-continuous bar complex computes derived Hom and Yoneda composition. The localization making Kc,FcK_c,F_c inverse on the proposed larger derived categories remains a further problem. [CQ7]

Coordinatewise tensor completion Defined in Chapter 8, 8.1 Tensor completion and matrix rank

Give the image the coordinatewise topology inherited from the full matrix space. Its completion is the full matrix space: finite-support matrices are dense, and the finite diagonal matrices converge coordinatewise to (δij)(\delta_{ij}). The identity matrix becomes available after this specified completion. Nothing in this calculation identifies the completion with a tensor product defined using a different topology.

Coproduct Defined in Chapter 2, 2.2 A coproduct gives the action on a tensor product

Suppose MM and NN are representations of the same algebra HH. Their vector-space tensor product exists, but an HH-action on it has not yet been specified. If we have a linear map

Δ:H⟶H⊗H,\Delta:H\longrightarrow H\otimes H,

we can try

h⋅(m⊗n)=∑h(1)m⊗h(2)n,Δ(h)=∑h(1)⊗h(2).h\cdot(m\otimes n) =\sum h_{(1)}m\otimes h_{(2)}n, \qquad \Delta(h)=\sum h_{(1)}\otimes h_{(2)}.
(2.1)

The notation on the right denotes a finite sum representing the algebraic tensor Δ(h)\Delta(h).

For (2.1) to be a representation, multiplication must be respected:

Δ(hh′)=Δ(h)Δ(h′),Δ(1H)=1H⊗1H.\Delta(hh')=\Delta(h)\Delta(h'),\qquad \Delta(1_H)=1_H\otimes1_H.
(2.2)

For three modules, the two resulting actions agree under the usual vector-space associator if

(Δ⊗id)Δ=(id⊗Δ)Δ.(\Delta\otimes\mathrm{id})\Delta =(\mathrm{id}\otimes\Delta)\Delta.
(2.3)

This is coassociativity. It compares two maps from HH to H⊗3H^{\otimes3}.

There is also a distinguished one-dimensional representation if we have an algebra map ϵ:H→k\epsilon:H\to k. It serves as the tensor unit when

(ϵ⊗id)Δ=id=(id⊗ϵ)Δ.(\epsilon\otimes\mathrm{id})\Delta =\mathrm{id} =(\mathrm{id}\otimes\epsilon)\Delta.
(2.4)

The map ϵ\epsilon is the coalgebra counit. An algebra HH with Δ\Delta and ϵ\epsilon satisfying (2.2)–(2.4) is a bialgebra.

The product–coproduct compatibility can be written as one equation between maps H⊗H→H⊗HH\otimes H\to H\otimes H:

Δm=(m⊗m)(id⊗τ⊗id)(Δ⊗Δ),\Delta m =(m\otimes m) (\mathrm{id}\otimes\tau\otimes\mathrm{id}) (\Delta\otimes\Delta),
(2.5)

where τ(a⊗b)=b⊗a\tau(a\otimes b)=b\otimes a. The middle interchange places the first components together and the second components together. This equation is the ordinary model for one of the compatibility problems in a chiral quantum group. The chiral problem must specify the position-dependent operation spaces and their interchange before it can assert the corresponding equation.

Determinant line Defined in Chapter 11, 11.1 Finite Gaussian integration and the determinant line

Their coordinate dependence is organized by the determinant line

Det⁡C=⨂j(det⁡Cj)(−1)j.\operatorname{Det}C =\bigotimes_j(\det C^j)^{(-1)^j}.

An exponent −1-1 means the dual line. The cotangent semidensity line in this construction is (Det⁡C)−1(\operatorname{Det}C)^{-1}. A semidensity transforms by the square root of the Berezinian, the graded analogue of a Jacobian. For a coefficient change AA, the cotangent lift has Berezinian (Ber⁡A)2(\operatorname{Ber}A)^2, and the transported semidensity acquires (Ber⁡A)−1(\operatorname{Ber}A)^{-1}. The determinant-line description fixes this factor without an independent square-root choice. The continued orientation of the even cycle is retained in a separate flat line. Determinant lines also provide the setting for regularized determinants of elliptic operators; Quillen's construction is a basic example. Quillen, Determinants of Cauchy–Riemann operators over a Riemann surface.

Differential module Defined in Chapter 3, 3.5 Differentiation and a change of coordinates

The coordinate zz made the mode calculation transparent. To move from a disc to a curve, one needs a way to differentiate sections and to compare their descriptions in different coordinates. The sheaf 𝒟X\mathcal D_X on a smooth curve XX is the sheaf of algebraic differential operators. On an affine coordinate chart its generators satisfy

[∂z,z]=1.[\partial_z,z]=1.

A left differential module, or left 𝒟X\mathcal D_X-module, is an 𝒪X\mathcal O_X-module MM with differentiation obeying the Leibniz rule

∇∂z(fm)=f′m+f∇∂zm.\nabla_{\partial_z}(fm)=f'm+f\nabla_{\partial_z}m.
(3.14)

For a vector bundle this is a connection. Differential modules may also be infinite-dimensional or supported on a subvariety, so they include more than vector bundles with connection.

On the coordinate line, a vector space with an operator TT gives the example M=𝒪X⊗VM=\mathcal O_X\otimes V with

∇∂z(f⊗v)=f′⊗v+f⊗Tv.\nabla_{\partial_z}(f\otimes v)=f'\otimes v+f\otimes Tv.

The equation records translation together with differentiation of scalar coefficients. It does not, on its own, give the response of a vertex algebra to every nonlinear coordinate change. To obtain a coordinate-independent construction on arbitrary curves, one supplies suitable coordinate-change actions; a conformal structure is a familiar way to obtain them. Translation-equivariant algebras on the affine line and coordinate-independent algebras on all curves are therefore different global assertions.

Chiral operations are conventionally written for right differential modules. If MM is a left module, its corresponding right module is

Mr=ωX⊗𝒪XM,M^{\mathrm r}=\omega_X\otimes_{\mathcal O_X}M,

where ωX\omega_X is the line bundle of one-forms. In a coordinate,

(dz⊗m)⋅∂z=−dz⊗∇∂zm.(dz\otimes m)\cdot\partial_z=-dz\otimes\nabla_{\partial_z}m.
(3.15)

This conversion accounts for the signs and one-form factors in a geometric residue. It is an equivalence between left and right differential modules; it is not a duality of the state spaces.

Factorization algebra Defined in Chapter 4, 4.4 Factorization includes the collision extension

In the classical algebraic formulation, a factorization algebra consists of quasi-coherent sheaves BIB_I on XIX^I, together with two kinds of identifications. A surjection π:J↠I\pi:J\twoheadrightarrow I gives the diagonal identification

νπ:Δπ∗BJ→∼BI\nu_\pi:\Delta_\pi^*B_J\xrightarrow{\sim}B_I
(4.7)

and the factorization identification on the block-separation open

cπ:⊠i∈IBJi|Uπ→∼BJ|Uπ.c_\pi: \left.\boxtimes_{i\in I}B_{J_i}\right|_{U_\pi} \xrightarrow{\sim} \left.B_J\right|_{U_\pi}.
(4.8)

The diagonal identifications compose under successive collapses. The factorization identifications compose under refinements of partitions, and these two systems agree when some clusters are collapsed while others remain separated. The sheaves have no nonzero local sections supported on the union of collision diagonals. A unit is a section 1∈B{1}1\in B_{\{1\}} whose external product with every local section extends across the two-point diagonal and restricts there to that section. These are the ordinary sheaf conditions of Chiral Algebras, §§3.4.2–3.4.4; in derived formulations the pullbacks, equivalences and compatibilities need their derived versions.

For example, taking BI=𝒪XIB_I=\mathcal O_{X^I} gives the unit factorization algebra. The factorization maps are the evident identifications of functions in separate sets of variables; the unit is the constant function 11. More interesting examples retain nontrivial collision data even though their restrictions to pairwise-distinct points are external products.

The full family is often described as a sheaf on the Ran space of XX. At the level of points, this is the set of finite nonempty subsets of XX; repeated labels specify the same subset. The maps Δπ\Delta_\pi express exactly those repetitions. One may use the compatible family (BI,νπ)(B_I,\nu_\pi) without treating the Ran space as an ordinary finite-dimensional variety.

Theorem: classical factorization and chiral algebras. The above category of unital factorization algebras is equivalent to the category of unital Beilinson–Drinfeld chiral algebras on XX. The factorization sheaves acquire a canonical differential-module structure, and the corresponding right differential module is ωX⊗B{1}\omega_X\otimes B_{\{1\}}.

This is Chiral Algebras, Proposition 3.4.7 and Theorem 3.4.9. The forward construction uses factorization to compare sections away from diagonals and then applies the geometric residue operation to obtain (4.3). The inverse construction is controlled by a complex indexed by partitions and their diagonals: its differential combines the chiral operations, and its exactness makes the collision extensions compatible. This partition complex is the Chevalley–Cousin complex of §§3.4.10–3.4.12. The theorem is about the full compatible sheaf data, including collisions and the unit. Giving only (4.8) on a separated open set omits part of its hypothesis.

The common domain is the coefficient-array intersection

LDfac(T)=LD(T)∩N1(T)=LR(T)∩N1(T).L_D^{\mathrm{fac}}(T)=L_D(T)\cap N_1(T)=L_R(T)\cap N_1(T).

Degree by degree, for each outer exponent jj, its sjs^j-coefficient belongs to T12((p))⊗M(j)T_{12}((p))\otimes M^{(j)} for some finite-dimensional graded subspace M(j)⊂M3M^{(j)}\subset M_3. Field Defined in Chapter 3, 3.1 Fields and their modes

Let VV be a complex vector space of states. A field on VV is a series

A(z)=∑n∈ℤAnz−n−1,An∈Endℂ⁡(V),A(z)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}A_nz^{-n-1}, \qquad A_n\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V),
(3.1)

such that, for each v∈Vv\in V, the vector AnvA_nv vanishes for all sufficiently large nn. The bound may depend on vv. Consequently A(z)vA(z)v belongs to V((z))V((z)): it has only finitely many negative powers of zz, although it may have infinitely many positive powers. The operators AnA_n are the modes of the field.

The coefficient notation is arranged so that

Anv=Resz=0⁡znA(z)vdz.A_n v=\operatorname{Res}_{z=0}z^n A(z)v\,dz.

Here the formal residue extracts the coefficient of z−1z^{-1}. No analytic integral is required for this definition. If a particular matrix coefficient is represented by a convergent meromorphic function, the same coefficient is its usual contour residue.

The products A(z)B(w)A(z)B(w) and B(w)A(z)B(w)A(z) initially have different expansion conventions. Their difference is interpreted as a two-variable formal distribution. Two fields are local if there is an integer N≥0N\geq0 such that

(z−w)N[A(z),B(w)]=0.(z-w)^N[A(z),B(w)]=0.
(3.2)

We are using even, or bosonic, fields; fields with odd parity require the corresponding graded commutator. Equation (3.2) says that multiplying by a sufficiently high power of the collision equation removes the difference between the two expansions. It does not assign a finite product at z=wz=w.

What happens if one inserts the flux twice? Write 𝔩=𝔤/ℂ1\mathfrak l=\mathfrak g/\mathbb C1, and lift each polynomial Weyl symbol to its representative with zero constant term. Geometric realization Defined in Chapter 13, 13.1 The realized vacuum on every configuration

Set 𝒞⌀=Vectℂ⁡\mathcal C_\varnothing=\operatorname{Vect}_{\mathbb C}. The vacuum at II is the object actually inserted from the empty set,

vI=β⌀→I(ℂ).v_I=\beta_{\varnothing\to I}(\mathbb C).

A geometric realization consists of 𝒪\mathcal O-linear functors

FI:𝒞I⟶QCoh⁡(XI)F_I:\mathcal C_I\longrightarrow\operatorname{QCoh}(X^I)

and comparisons with the finite-map functors and separated fusion. Here QCoh⁡\operatorname{QCoh} denotes quasi-coherent sheaves. Define the realized vacuum coefficients

BI=FI(vI).B_I=F_I(v_I).

Finally, the empty comparison must identify B⌀B_\varnothing with ℂ\mathbb C as a unital algebra. An identification of vector spaces alone does not fix the vacuum normalization.

These conditions give a factorization algebra BB. Its maps

Δπ∗BI⟶BJ,⊠jBIj|U⟶BI|U\Delta_\pi^*B_I\longrightarrow B_J, \qquad \left.\boxtimes_j B_{I_j}\right|_U \longrightarrow B_I|_U

are the images of actual categorical maps. The composition diagrams imply all their finite-set identities. The one-point vacuum is the map 𝒪X→B{1}\mathcal O_X\to B_{\{1\}}; there is no requirement that B{1}=𝒪XB_{\{1\}}=\mathcal O_X.

A:=Rec⁡(𝒞,F)=ωX⊗𝒪XB{1},A:=\operatorname{Rec}(\mathcal C,F) =\omega_X\otimes_{\mathcal O_X}B_{\{1\}},

as a right differential module. Its chiral product is determined by the two-point extension B{1,2}B_{\{1,2\}}. If j:X2∖Δ↪X2j:X^2\setminus\Delta\hookrightarrow X^2, the map is the composite

j∗j∗(A⊠A)⟶[j∗j∗(ωX⊠ωX)]⊗B{1,2}→Res⁡⊗1(Δ∗ωX)⊗B{1,2}⟶Δ∗A.\begin{aligned} j_*j^*(A\boxtimes A) &\longrightarrow \bigl[j_*j^*(\omega_X\boxtimes\omega_X)\bigr]\otimes B_{\{1,2\}}\\ &\xrightarrow{\operatorname{Res}\otimes1} (\Delta_*\omega_X)\otimes B_{\{1,2\}} \longrightarrow\Delta_*A. \end{aligned}

The first arrow uses separated factorization; the last uses the collision comparison. Thus the extension across the diagonal enters the formula itself. For an iterated collision, both orders tensor geometric residues with the same coefficient BIB_I. The finite-map and partition identities identify the two coefficient maps, so residue substitution gives every chiral operadic identity. On the affine line, translation equivariance gives the corresponding vertex algebra. A conformal vector is preserved when it is included in the input; it is not selected by an abstract tensor category. [GR1, GR2]

Hall correspondence Defined in Chapter 15, 15.1 Extensions and the reason for associativity

Let ℳα\mathcal M_\alpha be a moduli stack of objects of charge α\alpha. Here a charge is an additive class, such as a class in a Grothendieck group. Let ℰα,β\mathcal E_{\alpha,\beta} classify exact sequences with quotient of charge α\alpha and subobject of charge β\beta. The two maps are

ℳα×ℳβ← p ℰα,β→ q ℳα+β,p(M,B)=(M/B,B),q(M,B)=M.\mathcal M_\alpha\times\mathcal M_\beta \xleftarrow{\ p\ }\mathcal E_{\alpha,\beta} \xrightarrow{\ q\ }\mathcal M_{\alpha+\beta}, \qquad p(M,B)=(M/B,B),\quad q(M,B)=M.

Pullback along pp places the two inputs on the extension space; pushforward along qq combines all extensions with the same middle object. For constructible functions over ℂ\mathbb C, the resulting ordinary Hall product is

(f∗g)(M)=∫B⊂Mf(M/B)g(B)dχc.(f*g)(M)=\int_{B\subset M}f(M/B)g(B)\,d\chi_c.
(15.1)

The integral is the compactly supported Euler characteristic of the actual subobject varieties, weighted by the constructible function. We use finite charge support and domains on which this integral is defined. The indicator of the zero object is the unit. The order in (15.1) is quotient first, subobject second.

A small counting example explains why subobject geometry matters. In the category of vector spaces over 𝔽q\mathbb F_q, use finite counting in place of Euler integration, and let e1e_1 be the indicator of a one-dimensional space. Every extension of two one-dimensional vector spaces splits, but

(e1∗e1)(𝔽q2)=#ℙ1(𝔽q)=q2−1q−1=q+1.(e_1*e_1)(\mathbb F_q^2) =\#\mathbb P^1(\mathbb F_q) =\frac{q^2-1}{q-1}=q+1.

The product counts the lines inside the middle object. It does not count just the isomorphism classes of possible middle objects. Over ℂ\mathbb C, the constructible-function version gives χ(ℙ1)=2\chi(\mathbb P^1)=2.

(bz)(a)=az−za,(bf)(a1,a2)=a1f(a2)−f(a1a2)+f(a1)a2.(bz)(a)=az-za,\qquad (bf)(a_1,a_2)=a_1f(a_2)-f(a_1a_2)+f(a_1)a_2.

A class represented by a bimodule map A→A[n]A\to A[n] acts on a derived left module through

M≃A⊗ALM⟶A[n]⊗ALM≃M[n].M\simeq A\otimes_A^L M \longrightarrow A[n]\otimes_A^L M\simeq M[n].

Here differentials have degree +1+1, and V[1]j=Vj+1V[1]^j=V^{j+1}. The derived centre retains these operations and their coherent compositions. Homotopy Defined in Chapter 5, 5.1 Complexes retain the equations and their solutions

A chain map f:V→Wf:V\to W commutes with the differentials. A homotopy from gg to ff is a degree-minus-one map hh satisfying

f−g=dWh+hdV.f-g=d_Wh+hd_V.

Homotopic maps induce the same cohomology map, but the homotopy contains information that this induced map forgets. More generally, maps of all degrees form a complex

Homr⁡(V,W)=∏nHom⁡(Vn,Wn+r),∂f=dWf−(−1)rfdV.\operatorname{Hom}^r(V,W)=\prod_n\operatorname{Hom}(V^n,W^{n+r}), \qquad \partial f=d_Wf-(-1)^rfd_V.

Chain maps are its degree-zero cycles, and homotopies identify maps whose difference is a boundary. The product over nn is intentional: a degree-rr map has a component on every degree of VV.

A chain map is a quasi-isomorphism if it induces an isomorphism on every cohomology group. The ordinary derived category formally makes these maps invertible. We will also retain the derived mapping complexes, obtained by resolving the inputs as necessary, rather than keeping only their degree-zero cohomology. This enhanced form of the derived category remembers homotopies and homotopies between them; it is the meaning intended when the geometric theorem below refers to higher mapping spaces.

K-flat and K-injective Defined in Chapter 6, 6.1 What the unit and counit measure

A right dg module PP is K-flat if P⊗BXP\otimes_B X is acyclic whenever the left dg module XX is acyclic. Such a module computes derived tensor on arbitrary coefficients. Dually, a complex JJ is K-injective if its Hom complex from every acyclic complex is acyclic. Locality Defined in Chapter 3, 3.1 Fields and their modes

The products A(z)B(w)A(z)B(w) and B(w)A(z)B(w)A(z) initially have different expansion conventions. Their difference is interpreted as a two-variable formal distribution. Two fields are local if there is an integer N≥0N\geq0 such that

(z−w)N[A(z),B(w)]=0.(z-w)^N[A(z),B(w)]=0.
(3.2)

We are using even, or bosonic, fields; fields with odd parity require the corresponding graded commutator. Equation (3.2) says that multiplying by a sufficiently high power of the collision equation removes the difference between the two expansions. It does not assign a finite product at z=wz=w.

For example, write ιz,w\iota_{z,w} for expansion in nonnegative powers of w/zw/z, and ιw,z\iota_{w,z} for expansion in nonnegative powers of z/wz/w. Then

ιz,w1(z−w)2=∑r≥0(r+1)wrz−r−2,ιw,z1(z−w)2=∑r≥0(r+1)zrw−r−2.\iota_{z,w}\frac1{(z-w)^2} =\sum_{r\geq0}(r+1)w^rz^{-r-2}, \qquad \iota_{w,z}\frac1{(z-w)^2} =\sum_{r\geq0}(r+1)z^rw^{-r-2}.
(3.3)

These are expansions of the same rational function in two different regions. As formal distributions they are different. Multiplication by (z−w)2(z-w)^2 makes both equal to 11, so it kills their difference. This is the mechanism behind the locality equation for the current below.

Normalized boundary hypothesis Defined in Chapter 10, 10.1 Virasoro representations and domains of fields

Throughout the sewing results below, the normalized boundary hypothesis is retained: for algebraic external states, the two four-point inverse-Gram sewings converge in their respective channel discs, their marked channel vectors lie in the canonical spectral L2L^2 spaces, and the two are related by the specified real unitary fusion transformation. We also retain the normalized positive-label pentagon when comparing trees. These are substantive hypotheses. The role of quantum-group harmonic analysis in constructing fusion transformations is developed by Ponsot and Teschner, Liouville bootstrap via harmonic analysis on a noncompact quantum group (arXiv:hep-th/9911110); analytic continuation of fusion coefficients alone does not supply every completed-source estimate used here.

Products of two degree-minus-one homotopies vanish. Equations (16.9)–(16.10), with their mixed-degree versions, assemble into a coalgebra chain map on the bar construction. On a word, it sums over partitions into consecutive blocks of size one or two, applying Λ\Lambda to a singleton and KK to a pair. The triple identity is exactly the equality needed when a bar differential joins adjacent entries.

This also has an analytic completion theorem. Using the arithmetic ideal 𝒥a\mathcal J_a defined above, form the coefficient complex ℰ=[𝒥a→𝒜a]\mathcal E=[\mathcal J_a\to\mathcal A_a] in degrees −1,0-1,0. PR,N(x)=∑n≥0RnqN,π(xn),R>0,P_{R,N}(x)=\sum_{n\ge0}R^nq_{N,\pi}(x_n),\qquad R>0,

The estimate counts the same singleton/pair partitions. It extends the actual identities, not just a scalar trace, through the specified completion.

Locality asks for different structure. A supported coefficient can carry derivatives normal to a collision locus; a derived diagonal product also retains the classes measuring nontransverse intersection. Supported mapping complexes, such normal-jet sheaves, Gaussian preparation and completed finite-word comparisons are available. Their linking construction supplies a cyclic vector and nonlocal creation fields. It does not turn the linking algebra into a local field algebra.

Quasi-isomorphism Defined in Chapter 5, 5.1 Complexes retain the equations and their solutions

A chain map is a quasi-isomorphism if it induces an isomorphism on every cohomology group. The ordinary derived category formally makes these maps invertible. We will also retain the derived mapping complexes, obtained by resolving the inputs as necessary, rather than keeping only their degree-zero cohomology. This enhanced form of the derived category remembers homotopies and homotopies between them; it is the meaning intended when the geometric theorem below refers to higher mapping spaces.

Ribbon category Defined in Chapter 13

A tensor category records how representations combine, but it need not retain the local fields that act on them. A ribbon category also has dual objects, a braiding cM,N:M⊗N→N⊗Mc_{M,N}:M\otimes N\to N\otimes M, and a natural twist θM:M→M\theta_M:M\to M. The twist is compatible with the braiding and duality:

θM⊗N=cN,McM,N(θM⊗θN),θM∨=(θM)∨,\theta_{M\otimes N} =c_{N,M}c_{M,N}(\theta_M\otimes\theta_N),\qquad \theta_{M^\vee}=(\theta_M)^\vee,

with θ𝟏=1\theta_{\mathbf1}=1. The braiding satisfies the hexagons, and the evaluation and coevaluation maps satisfy the duality triangles.

Consider a positive-definite even integral lattice LL: a finite-rank free abelian group with integral symmetric pairing and (α,α)∈2ℤ(\alpha,\alpha)\in2\mathbb Z. Its lattice vertex algebra VLV_L is the direct sum of Heisenberg Fock spaces with charges α∈L\alpha\in L. The irreducible ordinary modules are indexed by L∗/LL^*/L, where

L∗={x∈L⊗ℝ:(x,L)⊂ℤ}.L^*=\{x\in L\otimes\mathbb R:(x,L)\subset\mathbb Z\}.

When LL is unimodular, L∗=LL^*=L, the vacuum is the only simple ordinary module. Its finite semisimple representation category is therefore the ribbon category of finite-dimensional vector spaces, with ordinary exchange and identity twist. The two even unimodular rank-sixteen lattices E8⊕︎E8E_8\oplus E_8 and D16+D_{16}^{+} give this same category. Their vertex algebras have central charge sixteen and the same torus character, but their weight-one current Lie algebras are different:

𝔢8⊕︎𝔢8and𝔰𝔬32.\mathfrak e_8\oplus\mathfrak e_8 \qquad\text{and}\qquad \mathfrak{so}_{32}.

Both have dimension 496496, and their nondegenerate scalar pairings are isometric over ℂ\mathbb C. The state-valued simple pole

Ja(z)Jb(w)∼(a,b)(z−w)2+J[a,b](w)z−wJ^a(z)J^b(w)\sim \frac{(a,b)}{(z-w)^2}+\frac{J^{[a,b]}(w)}{z-w}

distinguishes them. Recovering a chiral algebra therefore requires information about how its states extend across collisions. A ribbon category at one point does not contain that information by itself. [GR1]

We will examine three ways to retain it. A category-valued system on configurations has a geometric vacuum whose coefficients reconstruct the chiral algebra. Supported duality compares entire collision complexes, with its reversal of arrows kept explicit. Finite rational categories admit a different reconstruction over a finite-dimensional base algebra. Their successes have different hypotheses, and their comparison is a mathematical question.

ej⟼∑α(i)=jei.e_j\longmapsto\sum_{\alpha(i)=j}e_i .

An adjunction provides comparison maps. Whether those maps are equivalences requires a theorem about the objects and weak equivalences under consideration. The geometry of ordered configurations supplies an especially useful finiteness condition for such a theorem.

Upward-proper support Defined in Chapter 9, 9.2 Fields as joint currents

This coefficient complex has two polarizations, called xx and pp. An internal mixed form of degree rr has cohomological degree r−2r-2 in the xx-polarization and r−1r-1 in the pp-polarization. On every compact set of external parameters, the xx-variables have a common compact support. A pp-variable can extend upward in height, but above a common collar height its current is independent of that height and has no dtdt-component. This is the meaning of upward-proper support here. Particle number is finite, and these finite operations are defined over ℂ[ℏ]\mathbb C[\hbar].

Vertex algebra Defined in Chapter 3, 3.2 A vertex algebra retains states and local products

A vertex algebra packages a compatible family of fields on one state space. In the even convention used here, its data are a vector space VV, a vacuum vector 𝟏\mathbf1, a translation operator T:V→VT:V\to V, and a linear assignment

a⟼Y(a,z)=∑n∈ℤa(n)z−n−1a\longmapsto Y(a,z)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}a_{(n)}z^{-n-1}

of a field to every state aa. They satisfy the vacuum and creation identities

Y(𝟏,z)=idV⁡,Y(a,z)𝟏∈a+zV[[z]],Y(\mathbf1,z)=\operatorname{id}_V, \qquad Y(a,z)\mathbf1\in a+zV[[z]],
(3.4)

the translation identities

T𝟏=0,[T,Y(a,z)]=∂zY(a,z)=Y(Ta,z),T\mathbf1=0, \qquad [T,Y(a,z)]=\partial_zY(a,z)=Y(Ta,z),
(3.5)

and locality for every pair Y(a,z),Y(b,w)Y(a,z),Y(b,w). These conditions express the state–field correspondence, the infinitesimal motion of an insertion, and the compatibility of products at distinct positions. They imply

Y(a,z)𝟏=ezTa,a=a(−1)𝟏.Y(a,z)\mathbf1=e^{zT}a, \qquad a=a_{(-1)}\mathbf1.

Thus the vacuum connects an operator-valued field with the state it creates. It has not yet supplied a scalar-valued vacuum expectation: that requires a linear functional or pairing in addition.

The singular part of the product is written

Y(a,z)Y(b,w)∼∑n≥0Y(a(n)b,w)(z−w)n+1.Y(a,z)Y(b,w) \sim\sum_{n\geq0} \frac{Y(a_{(n)}b,w)}{(z-w)^{n+1}}.
(3.6)

The symbol ∼\sim means equality of singular parts in the indicated expansion convention. The sum is finite for each pair of states. The regular coefficients also belong to the vertex-algebra structure: in particular, a(−1)ba_{(-1)}b defines the normally ordered product. Retaining only (3.6) therefore retains less information than the full state–field map.

One can collect the singular coefficients into a polynomial in a formal variable λ\lambda:

[aλb]=∑n≥0λnn!a(n)b.[a_\lambda b]=\sum_{n\geq0}\frac{\lambda^n}{n!}a_{(n)}b.
(3.7)

This λ\lambda-bracket is convenient for differential identities. It records the singular products; it is not, by itself, a definition of the full vertex algebra. Beilinson and Drinfeld relate vertex algebras to translation-equivariant chiral algebras on the affine line in Chiral Algebras, §0.15, and express the state–field operation geometrically in §3.5.

Weak Hopf algebra Defined in Chapter 13, 13.5 Finite rational categories and a non-scalar base

Writing VaV_a for the underlying vector space of F(La)F(L_a), reconstruction gives a finite weak Hopf algebra

H=⨁a∈IEndℂ⁡(Va).H=\bigoplus_{a\in I}\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V_a).

The coproduct can be written using the tensor comparison JJ. Let π\pi project the ordinary tensor onto the relative tensor over BB, and let

ι(v⊗Bw)=∑ivei⊗eiw.\iota(v\otimes_Bw)=\sum_i ve_i\otimes e_iw.

Put m=Jπm=J\pi and s=ιJ−1s=\iota J^{-1}. If hMh_M denotes the natural action of hh on F(M)F(M), then

Δ(h)M,N=sM,NhM⊠NmM,N,ε(h)=λ(h𝟏∑iei),λ(ei)=1.\Delta(h)_{M,N}=s_{M,N}h_{M\boxtimes N}m_{M,N}, \qquad \varepsilon(h)=\lambda\!\left(h_{\mathbf1}\sum_i e_i\right), \quad\lambda(e_i)=1.

“Weak” refers to its unit and counit identities: the coproduct is coassociative and multiplicative, but Δ(1)\Delta(1) need not be 1⊗11\otimes1, and the scalar counit need not be multiplicative. The tensor of representations is

Δ(1)(V⊗W),Δ(1)=∑i∈Iρi⊗ℓi,\Delta(1)(V\otimes W), \qquad \Delta(1)=\sum_{i\in I}\rho_i\otimes\ell_i,

where ρi,ℓi\rho_i,\ell_i are right and left actions of the idempotent ei∈Be_i\in B. This projection is exactly intermediate-label matching. The reconstruction preserves the ribbon structure and the finite pairing tensor. [GR7]

Weil functional Defined in Chapter 16, 16.1 The complete arithmetic functional

Use logarithmic scale u=log⁡xu=\log x, so multiplication of positive scales becomes addition. For a test f∈Cc∞(ℝ)f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R), set

fˆ(z)=∫ℝf(u)eizudu,Hf(s)=∫ℝf(u)e(s−1/2)udu=fˆ(−i(s−1/2)).\widehat f(z)=\int_{\mathbb R}f(u)e^{izu}\,du, \qquad H_f(s)=\int_{\mathbb R}f(u)e^{(s-1/2)u}\,du =\widehat f(-i(s-1/2)).

Convolution and involution are

(f∗g)(u)=∫f(t)g(u−t)dt,f∗(u)=f(−u).(f*g)(u)=\int f(t)g(u-t)\,dt, \qquad f^*(u)=\overline{f(-u)}.

The complete Weil functional, in this normalization, is

W(f)=Hf(0)+Hf(1)−f(0)log⁡π+12π∫ℝfˆ(r)Re⁡ψ(1/4+ir/2)dr−∑n≥2Λ(n)n(f(log⁡n)+f(−log⁡n)),\begin{aligned} W(f)={}&H_f(0)+H_f(1)-f(0)\log\pi\\ &+\frac1{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb R}\widehat f(r) \operatorname{Re}\psi(1/4+ir/2)\,dr\\ &-\sum_{n\ge2}\frac{\Lambda(n)}{\sqrt n} \bigl(f(\log n)+f(-\log n)\bigr), \end{aligned}
(16.1)

where ψ=Γ′/Γ\psi=\Gamma'/\Gamma, Λ(pk)=log⁡p\Lambda(p^k)=\log p, and Λ(n)=0\Lambda(n)=0 otherwise. The first two terms are the polar contributions, the integral is part of the real-place contribution, and the last sum contains both orientations of every prime power. For instance, each of f(log⁡4)f(\log4) and f(−log⁡4)f(-\log4) has coefficient −log⁡2/2-\log2/2, since 4=224=2^2. [The test algebra and its scalar functional][trace-foundations]

The completed zeta function

ξ(s)=12s(s−1)π−s/2Γ(s/2)ζ(s)\xi(s)=\tfrac12s(s-1)\pi^{-s/2}\Gamma(s/2)\zeta(s)

is entire. Let ρ\rho run through its distinct zeros, let mρm_\rho be the multiplicity, and write wρ=−i(ρ−1/2)w_\rho=-i(\rho-1/2). The explicit formula identifies (16.1) with

W(f)=∑ρmρfˆ(wρ).W(f)=\sum_\rho m_\rho\widehat f(w_\rho).
(16.2)

The decay of the transform and the zero-counting bound give convergence on the stated test class. Formula (16.1), however, can be defined without knowing any zero individually. This distinction is the starting point for a geometric trace construction.

Weil positivity Defined in Chapter 16, 16.1 The complete arithmetic functional

Positivity concerns the quadratic form

Q(g)=W(g∗g∗).Q(g)=W(g*g^*).
(16.3)

Since g∗g∗ˆ(z)=gˆ(z)gˆ(z‾)\widehat{g*g^*}(z)=\widehat g(z)\overline{\widehat g(\bar z)}, a real wρw_\rho contributes mρ|gˆ(wρ)|2m_\rho|\widehat g(w_\rho)|^2. A nonreal point does not contribute an absolute square. The Weil positivity criterion equates Q(g)≥0Q(g)\ge0 for every compact smooth complex test with the Riemann hypothesis. Thus the all-test quantifier is part of the mathematical problem, not a harmless extension of a finite calculation.

§1 · Orientation

How the programme fits together

An associative chiral algebra comes with a choice of configuration tensor. For coefficients indexed by words, multiplication uses consecutive cuts. The ordered collision atlas allows every ordered decomposition into subsets. At two separated labels there can already be two atlas summands and just one chosen word summand. A Beilinson–Drinfeld chiral Lie bracket instead takes its value on the diagonal and obeys the Jacobi identity.

The bar construction records products and their homotopies as a coalgebra. For a connected coefficient algebra on either prescribed tensor, positive words on nn labels have length at most nn. This finite filtration is the reason cobar can recover even unbounded coefficient complexes arity by arity. To recognize a second boundary algebra one must transpose the coproduct into a product of the correct variance and identify the second boundary independently.

A quantum group can be recovered from a category of lines together with a faithful tensor functor. For Ising the tensor functor remembers three simple boundary labels. Their matching projection specifies the tensor product. Keeping a marked half-turn also determines the orientation of the spin braiding.

A filling assigns a linear functional or a vector to the boundary. Which state it prepares depends on the action, integration cycle, source and sewing operation. For the harmonic disk these data determine mixed moments of distinct modes. A proposed gravity reconstruction must supply its own measure, spatial cut and probes.

Fields and their representations

Free currents, affine and Virasoro systems, WW-algebras and quantum vertex algebras test duality, module localization, exchange and fusion on concrete algebraic or completed carriers.

Families of examples

  • Heisenberg, free fields and lattice vertex algebras
  • Affine Kac–Moody algebras at irrational shifted level
  • Affine algebras at rational level
  • Affine algebras at critical level
  • Virasoro algebras, finite categories and continuous series
  • WW-algebras and quantum Drinfeld–Sokolov reduction
  • Yangians, the Yang double and rational quantum vertex algebras
  • Trigonometric and elliptic spectral parameters

Geometry, Hall algebras and branes

Hall correspondences, Hilbert schemes, matrix complexes, Miura algebras, compact K3 coefficients and symplectic examples have substantial algebraic and geometric theories. Their further comparisons must preserve proper operations, parity, orientation and untraced states.

Families of examples

  • Hall algebras and shuffle algebras
  • D3 branes and Hilbert-scheme vertex algebras
  • M2 branes and the two-matrix algebra
  • M5 branes, Miura algebras and surface fusion
  • K3 surfaces, compact Hall theory and the Igusa form
  • The six-sphere and symplectic local examples

Bulk observables, defects and gravity

Celestial currents, higher-dimensional gauge theories and gravity require independently constructed bulk actions, line or surface operations, analytic sewing and source-dependent state preparation.

Families of examples

  • Celestial algebras of self-dual gauge theory
  • Celestial self-dual gravity and the Moyal deformation
  • Three-dimensional gravity and Liouville theory
  • Six-dimensional holomorphic Chern–Simons theory
  • Four-dimensional Chern–Simons theory

Arithmetic traces and integral coefficients

The arithmetic branch has continuous spectral duality, integral normal/Frobenius operations and a geometric representative of the complete Weil trace. It asks for a common proper trace domain, further native field comparisons and signed positivity on every whole test window.

Families of examples

  • Arithmetic: Weil positivity, spectral duality and integral jets

How to read the page

Choose a physical operation
For a charged line use the Heisenberg family. For a tensor product over a finite base use Virasoro. The Hall family describes composition by a flag of subobjects.
Identify the coefficient space
An ordinary direct sum, a fixed-precision quotient and an inverse limit admit different elements. The operation must be defined on the actual output of the preceding step.
Follow a collision
A measures transport around the diagonal. The map attaching a point coefficient to the link determines how the sheaf extends across it.
Identify the state
A vacuum in an algebra fixes a local insertion. A is specified by a filling and its normalization. Their roles meet in a sewing identity.
